title: Rear pullets for table egg production

lessons.title: Rearing pullets: growth and uniformity
lessons.html:
Rearing pullets: growth and uniformity

A pullet is a young female chicken that has not started laying. Pullets are reared from day-old until they are moved to the laying house. How well a pullet is reared decides how well she will lay for the rest of her life.

Goals of rearing

  • Pullets reach the target body weight for their age, as shown in the breed guide.
  • The flock is even (uniform): most birds are close to the average weight.
  • Birds are healthy and fully vaccinated before they start laying.
  • Birds start laying at the planned age, not too early or too late.

Feeding stages

Pullets get different feeds as they grow, such as chick starter, grower and developer, then a pre-lay feed before laying. Give only the feed your supervisor plans. Feeding too much makes fat birds; too little makes small birds that lay small eggs.

Weighing and uniformity

  1. Weigh a sample of birds from different parts of the house regularly, often weekly.
  2. Write down every weight.
  3. The supervisor compares the average with the breed target and checks how many birds are close to the average.

If the flock is uneven, small birds may not get enough feeder space. Check that feed reaches all feeders quickly and that there is enough feeder and drinker space for all birds to eat at once.

Space and beak care

Crowded pullets peck each other. Keep to the stocking density set by the farm. Any beak treatment is done only by trained people at the age the farm sets.

lessons.title: Lighting, vaccination and moving to the laying house
lessons.html:
Lighting, vaccination and moving to the laying house

Lighting programme

Day length controls when pullets start laying. During rearing the light hours are usually kept short and steady so birds do not start laying too early. Before laying, light hours are increased step by step to start egg production. The farm manager sets the programme from the breed guide.

  • Never change the light clock on your own.
  • Check that lights switch on and off at the set times.
  • Report broken bulbs and light leaks in curtains.

Never decrease the light hours once birds are laying; this can make them stop.

Vaccination

Pullets get many vaccines during rearing to protect them for their laying life. The vet sets the programme.

  • Keep vaccines cold and use them before expiry.
  • Use the method shown: eye drop, water, spray or injection.
  • Record the date, vaccine, batch and house.
  • Report birds that react badly after vaccination.

Moving to the laying house

  1. Prepare the laying house: clean, disinfected, with water, feed and lights working.
  2. Move birds at the age planned, before laying starts.
  3. Catch birds gently in dim light. Hold them correctly and never by the neck or one wing.
  4. Do not overfill crates and keep them in shade.
  5. Make sure birds find water quickly in the new house. Check nipple lines.
  6. Record numbers moved and deaths.

Moving is stressful. Keep the birds calm and follow the same feed and light plan the manager sets.

Key points

  • A well-reared pullet becomes a good layer.
  • Aim for target weight and an even flock.
  • Light hours control the start of lay; never change them on your own.
  • Complete all vaccinations before laying and record them.
  • Move pullets gently and make sure they find water quickly.
